title: Korea's lay founders (1784)
hook: Korean scholars read Christian books and founded their own church before any priest arrived

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japan's kakure kirishitan, keeping prayers by heart with no priests. Your line was hidden, but kept. Did you keep your small practice with nobody watching? Day nine hundred ten.

A handful of Korean scholars sit together over a pile of books. They are Confucian men, trained to read closely and argue carefully, and these books have come to them from Beijing, written in classical Chinese, the language of learning they all share. Some of the books are about astronomy and mathematics. Some are about a Lord of Heaven. No missionary has handed them over. No preacher is in the room. They are simply reading, and arguing, and reading again. What they did next is the story. Today: Korea's lay founders.

Among the books, the accounts say, was one written in Chinese by Matteo Ricci, the Jesuit from two days ago, about the Lord of Heaven. The scholars studied it the way they studied everything: closely. One of them, Yi Seung-hun, traveled to Beijing with a mission from the Korean court, found the Catholic church there, and asked to be baptized. He took the name Peter. When he came home, he baptized his friends. And so a church began in Korea led entirely by laypeople, ordinary believers, not clergy. They met in homes, read together, and shared what they learned. For a while they even chose some of their own to lead worship as priests do, until they learned from the bishop in Beijing that only an ordained priest could do that, and they stopped. Acts describes some early believers who "received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily". These scholars did something like it, with no priest at their side. It cost them. The faith was soon outlawed, and persecutions came again and again. When a priest finally did arrive, he found a church already there. Catholics in Korea remember these founders and martyrs with honor. Look back at this whole week. Las Casas arguing against conquest. Mary at Guadalupe, in Catholic telling. Martin with his broom, Kateri in the woods, Ricci in scholar's robes, the hidden Christians in Japan. The faith met new peoples in very different ways. Here it arrived as a book, and readers did the rest.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read, and share what you learn. Sit comfortably, and let the room go quiet. Bring to mind one thing you've learned on this path that stayed with you. A line, a story, a person from this week maybe. Say it to yourself in one sentence, plainly, the way you'd tell a friend at dinner. Then think of who might like to hear it. If you pray, you can pray for that person. If you don't, just hold their name. The bell holds the time.
cheonju. Korean for the Lord of Heaven, the name for God that Korean scholars found in a book from Beijing and used to start a church led by laypeople.
Your line: the laity began it. Today, share your one sentence with that person, in a message or over a meal. Just the sentence, no sermon. Day nine hundred ten.

howItsDone: Catholics in Korea honor their founders and martyrs, visit shrines connected with them, and point to the church's lay beginnings as part of who they are.

notes: Claims rule: no year or counts in the spoken text (the index title keeps 1784).

Ricci's Tianzhu shiyi among the books read in Korea; Yi Seung-hun baptized in Beijing as Peter; the lay community appointing its own 'priests' and stopping on the bishop's word; persecution; a priest (Zhou Wenmo) arriving later to find a church: confirm against Dallet and modern histories.
Week-end look-back covers days 904–909 (and Martin de Porres, 906); Guadalupe is framed as Catholic telling.
Editor pass: 'with no one to guide them' changed to 'with no priest at their side', since the script itself says they took guidance from the bishop in Beijing.
Second editor pass: practice opener varied ('Settle, and breathe' was repeated across days 908–916).
